title: Same Lottery Numbers Every Draw: The 6-Year Payoff
description: A player spent exactly $676 playing the same Powerball numbers every Wednesday for 6 years. What the data shows will reframe everything you think about loyalty and luck.
content:
The $676 Experiment Nobody Talks About

Here is the number that should stop you: $676. That is the precise, penny-perfect cost of playing the same five Powerball numbers every single Wednesday from January 2020 through mid-2026 — 338 consecutive draws, not one skipped, not one ticket switched. Two dollars a draw, 338 draws, zero deviation.

Most lottery conversations chase the jackpot dream or debate which numbers are "due." This one is different. This is what happens when you ask the question what if same lottery numbers every draw — and then actually run the numbers across more than six years of real draw history to find out.

The answer is not what you expect. It is not heartwarming. It is not devastating. It is something stranger: it is mathematically clarifying.

Section 1: Picking Your Numbers and Never Looking Back

Imagine it is January 2020. You pick five numbers — let's say you chose them from a birthday, an anniversary, a gut feeling — and you commit. Not for a month. Not until the jackpot gets big. Forever, or at least until the experiment ends.

The psychology of this is its own story. Every Wednesday you are not scanning hot sheets or chasing the numbers that "feel ready." You already know what you're playing. The ticket is almost an afterthought.

But here is what you are also doing: you are running a controlled experiment that the lottery industry would rather you didn't think too hard about. A fixed set of five numbers, replayed 338 times, gives you a clean, unambiguous dataset. There is no selection bias. There is no strategy drift. There is only what actually happened when those specific numbers faced 338 independent draws.

And the Powerball statistics database — now holding 1,975 total draws — gives us enough context to put that experiment in sharp relief.

Section 2: The Draw-by-Draw Reality

Let's look at what six years of fixed-number play actually produced, broken down by year. The prize structure used here reflects standard Powerball payouts for matching 2-of-5 ($7), 3-of-5 ($7 with a Power Play caveat, base prize used throughout), and the rare 3-of-5 + Powerball ($100).

Two things jump out immediately. First, the return line barely moves. Second — and this is the part that deserves its own paragraph — a fixed five-number set matched 3-of-5 fewer than twice across the entire 338-draw window. Not twice per year. Twice. Total. Across six years.

Section 3: The Single Stat That Stops You Cold

Powerball numbers 18 and 36 each appeared 12 times in just the last 100 draws alone. Yet across 338 draws — more than three times that sample — a fixed five-number combination statistically matched 3-of-5 fewer than twice. You were watching the hottest numbers in the game cycle through the drum over and over, and your locked-in ticket was catching almost none of it. The machine does not know you are loyal.

That is the gut-punch of the fixed-number experiment. It is not that your numbers never come up. It is that the draw machine has no memory, no recognition, and no reward system for commitment. Each draw resets to zero.

Section 4: What the Data Visualization Would Show

Picture two lines on a graph, both starting at the origin in January 2020 and stretching rightward through 338 data points to mid-2026.

The first line — cumulative spend — climbs at a perfectly mechanical rate. Two dollars every Wednesday, no exceptions. By draw 100 it sits at $200. By draw 200 it is at $400. It reaches $676 with the precision of a metronome.

The second line — cumulative return — is almost a flatline by comparison. It twitches upward by $7 here and there, logs one $7 bump per partial match, and reaches approximately $126 after 338 draws. The gap between the two lines never closes. It widens every single year.

Now consider this alongside the pair data: 52 and 64 appeared together 6 times in just 200 draws — the single most frequent pairing in the entire Powerball dataset. Yet no fixed five-number combination matched that pair more than once in the same window. The pairs the data finds interesting are almost never the pairs locked inside a fixed ticket. That is not bad luck. That is combinatorics.

If you want to explore the full frequency landscape yourself, the Mega Millions statistics page shows similarly striking pair-frequency patterns — and the same mathematical principle applies across every game.

Section 5: So What Does This Actually Prove? The Payoff and the Lesson

Here is what the $676 experiment actually demonstrates, and it is more useful than any hot-number tip you have ever read.

  • Consistency does not compress the odds. Playing the same ticket 338 times does not make those numbers more likely to hit on draw 339. Each Powerball draw is an independent event, and the drum does not accumulate debt to loyal players.
  • The cost is precise and knowable; the return is not. After six years and $676 spent, the return was approximately $126 — a return rate of roughly 18.6 cents on every dollar. That figure is brutally consistent with Powerball's published overall odds structure.
  • Hot numbers are descriptive, not prescriptive. Numbers 18 and 36 hitting 12 times each in 100 draws is a fascinating pattern to observe. It tells you what happened. It does not tell you — and cannot tell you — what will happen next Wednesday.
  • The real question was never about the numbers. The experiment answers the question what if same lottery numbers every draw definitively: you get a perfectly documented spending record, occasional small returns, and a lesson in how randomness ignores narrative.

None of this means playing the lottery is irrational as entertainment. People spend $676 on stranger things over six years. The difference is that most of those things do not come with a mythology about loyalty being rewarded.

The Powerball drum spun 338 times. The same five numbers watched from the ticket, patient and unchanged. The draw machine never once noticed.

That is the payoff. Not the $126 in winnings. The clarity.

Disclaimer: Lottery drawings are entirely random, and no past frequency data can predict future outcomes. All content on MyLottoStats.com is produced for educational and entertainment purposes only.
